Calveno — Improv Reference

Quick-build tools for names, locations, and NPCs that fit the city. Use when the party goes somewhere you didn’t prep.

Linguistic Roots

CultureRootFeel
Calveno humanNorthern Italian / VenetianMelodic, vowel-ending, names that sound like a trade city evolved them over centuries
TessarineElevated Italian / Genoese nobleLonger, more formal, surnames that imply old money and lineage
RattkinShort Anglo + descriptor surnameOne syllable or two; surname is a visible physical trait
Canal city halflingAbsorbed Italian first names, Anglo surnamesFirst names match the city; surnames stayed from wherever they came from

Location Naming

Calveno places are named from observable facts, not mythology.

Patterns:

StructureExampleMeaning
Al + nounAl Fondale”at the bottom”
La + nounLa Vasca”the basin”
Il + nounIl Bivio”the fork”
Casa + descriptorCasa Lupo”wolf house”
Ponte + descriptorPonte Bassa”low bridge”
Studio + surnameStudio Orsiniowner’s name
Acqua + colourAcqua Nera”black water”

Useful Italian nouns for places: Arco (arch), Bivio (fork), Corda (rope), Ferro (iron), Fondo (bottom), Gatta (cat), Muro (wall), Passo (pass), Rosso (red), Sasso (stone), Stretto (narrow), Trave (beam), Vento (wind)

Urban vocabulary (Venetian):

WordWhat it describes
CalleNarrow lane between buildings
FondamentaCanal-side walkway
RioInner city canal
CampoSmall square
SotoportegoCovered passage through a building
RugaWider lane with shops on both sides

11Tessarine factor’s secretary — following a schedule, not talking

d10Trait

4Watching the water, not the crowd

d10Want
1Someone to take the other end of this rope

6To warn a stranger about the prank team that’s been following them

Free Information (DC 8–10 Persuasion)

  • The boat three moorings down hasn’t moved in four days.
  • A Canal Commission inspector was measuring a maintenance hatch at dawn with a knotted cord and no lantern.
  • That Beffa team registered under a name in a Verdant Teeth dialect.
  • Three low hulls have been sitting in the outer roads with no pennant. Too clean for fishing boats.
  • There’s a buyer on the Bridge’s top tier paying well for Red Lady survivor accounts.
  • Nona Black-Jaw’s kitchen door has been busy this week.
  • A Warren Kin runner came through Le Paludi at an unusual hour.

District Atmosphere

DistrictTexture
MercaturaVoices overlap; boats press in from both sides; the stone is warm from all-day sun.
The BridgeThe arch puts everyone in shadow; the vendors at the base haven’t looked up all morning.
Le PaludiNarrow enough to hear the neighbour’s kettle through the wall; the water barely moves.
Velo QuarterTwo songs at once; lanterns lit even now; nobody explains what they’re celebrating.
Arsenal approachThe pitch smell comes before the walls; a guard with a ledger watches everything on the water.
Outer harbourSalt and wind; the city noise drops; boats sit at anchor with no one asking questions yet.

Canal textures (d6):

RollCanal looks like…
1Narrow — walls close on both sides; two boats cannot pass without touching
2Covered — stone arch overhead, no direct light, green and echoing
3Contested — a loaded barge blocks the flow; boats queue behind it
4Quiet residential spur — a dead end; this water doesn’t reach the main canal
5Broad artery — three boats wide; pilots calling across the lanes
6Bridge-crossed — low span above; vendors have claimed both railings

How Calvenans Talk

Every conversation in Calveno has a transaction under it, stated or implied.

Common openings:

  • “Who sent you?” — before answering anything useful
  • “That’s not cheap.” — before the price
  • “Someone will have heard about this.” — before helping with something private
  • “Let’s say—” — before a number
  • “I know a man.” / “I know a woman.” — before a referral
  • “Paid in full, witnessed, no argument.” — closing a deal

Common hedges:

  • “You understand I can’t—” (then does the thing, for a price)
  • “That’s between you and whoever you’re asking about.” (not a refusal; an invitation)
  • “I only remember boats.” (deniability; they remember everything)

Tessarine voice: More patient, more formal. They wait. They record.

  • “I wonder if you’ve considered—” (a better offer that serves them more)
  • “That’s already in our ledger.” (they know more than you thought)
  • “Naturally, we’d be happy to facilitate—” (a condition is coming)

Rattkin voice (Warren, Passage, Black-Jaw): Direct, concrete, no performance.

  • “What do you need.” (not a question)
  • “That costs a favour.” (specific currency; they track these)
  • “Nona will know.” (sometimes a warning, sometimes a reassurance)
